The Supreme Court will review the administration's mandatory detention policy for people in the country illegally, and Paris Kerry Johnson has the latest.
The Trump administration reinterpreted in 1996 law to deny bond hearings to migrants who have sometimes been in the U.S. for decades. Lower courts mostly rejected that approach and ruled the migrants deserve a chance to remain free while their cases move through the immigration system.
The ACLU says millions of people could be affected by the Trump policy, most with no criminal record. Now the U.S. Supreme Court will add the case to its docket.
The White House says the courts have been flooded with petitions from migrants, and the current process is unworkable and disruptive. The high court recently agreed to consider another key immigration issue, whether the administration can send migrants to countries where they have no prior tie.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
The co-pilot accused of sabotaging a Dubai to Tel Aviv flight is from Oman, that today from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. And Paris Kat Lonstarov says that revelation's raising questions about the pilot vetting process.
Israel does not allow pilots from countries it doesn't have diplomatic relations with to fly into its airspace. That includes Oman.
Speaking on Fox News, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Israel checks the background of pilots flying routes into the country.
He said that this pilot must have gotten through a quote loophole.
Israeli officials have said the incident was an attempted terrorist attack, although the motive is still unknown.
The United Arab Emirates says it's opened an investigation into what happened on the flight. Israel says it's participating in that.
Both the pilot and the co-pilot are alive and being questioned. Kat Lonstarov, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
Authorities say the co-pilot stabbed and injured the captain, who is reported to be an Indian citizen. This is NPR.
A new crew is en route to the International Space Station after the launch from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida on NASA's Crew-13 mission.
Central Florida Public Media's Brendan Byrne has details.
The crew of four includes two NASA astronauts, one from Canada and a Russian cosmonaut.
They launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket aboard the company's Crew Dragon capsule.
It will take the crew only about eight hours to arrive at the station, the fastest travel time to the ISS by a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule.
They'll spend nearly half a year living and working on the station, performing science experiments from the orbiting lab, some even on themselves.
This crew is replacing four people who have been on the station since February. They'll make the trip back home early next week, splashing down off the coast of Southern California.
For NPR News, I'm Brendan Byrne at the Kennedy Space Center.
Vice President J. D. Vance hits the campaign trail in Florida this hour as he and President Trump stump for Republicans in congressional races less than five weeks before the midterm elections.
President Trump's on a mission to energize Republican voters in the deep red states of Texas and then Oklahoma.
More Republicans in close House and Senate races have distanced themselves from Trump.
He faces low public approval ratings over the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gasoline and diesel prices,
although today AAA notes that the price of gas has ticked down. The Congressional Budget Office has directly linked the war to higher inflation.
